index.lead: These are the tools for writing Nucleus Co-op handlers. They check a handler for the mistakes Nucleus doesn't warn you about, show what each player would get before you start a game, and put the docs for every option where you're typing.
index.path: Every tool covers writing, checking and Try it. What comes after differs from tool to tool, and the comparison shows how.

start.md: Open [the workbench](@docs:tools/workbench) and do [Learn](@site:learn/), which builds a first handler with you. You can ignore the rest of this page for now.
Get the tools for the editor you use: [Notepad++](@docs:tools/notepadpp) or [VS Code](@docs:tools/vscode). They check your handler while you type and can start Nucleus Co-op with it.

start.who: You use another editor, a terminal or an AI agent

core.line: They're all built on the same core, so you get the same checks and the same Try it result whichever one you use.

editorsPage.title: Compare the editors
editorsPage.desc: VS Code, Notepad++, other editors and the workbench side by side, and what each one can do.
editorsPage.lead: All of these give you the same checks, fixes, suggestions and docs, because they share one core. They differ in how you install them, and in what they can do once the handler is written: debugging, saving, and testing in Nucleus Co-op. The table below has the details.

pick.title: VS Code
pick.line: The only one with a Docs panel, Try it next to your code and a debugger all in the editor. If you don't have a favourite, pick this one.

pick.title: Notepad++
pick.line: The most popular editor among handler authors. Setup is a double-click. It has no debugger.

tools.title: Workbench
tools.what: The workbench is a handler editor that runs in your browser. It checks your handler while you type, shows what Nucleus would set up for each player, lets you step through the code, and keeps the docs next to it.
when: You want to write or fix a handler right now and don't want to install anything.
You're new to handlers. The tour, the Lines list, the tips and Learn are there to help.
You already write handlers and want to check a quick change, or open one somebody sent you as a link.
You're curious how a handler on the Hub works. Open it and run Check and Try it on it.
You're not at your own PC. Any modern browser will do, a phone included.
tools.not: One thing it can't do is start Nucleus Co-op, because browsers aren't allowed to start programs. For one-click testing in Nucleus, use VS Code, Notepad++ or `ncdev test`.

tools.title: VS Code
tools.desc: What the VS Code extension does, with its commands, keys and settings.
tools.what: The extension adds handler support to VS Code and VSCodium. Problems are underlined while you type and come with quick fixes. You also get suggestions, docs on hover and in a side panel, Try it, a debugger, and commands that package a handler, install it and start Nucleus Co-op with it.
when: You write handlers regularly and want everything in one place.
You already use VS Code for other things.
You want breakpoints and stepping in VS Code's own Run and Debug.
You use Copilot or another agent in VS Code. The extension gives it the Nucleus tools.
tools.videoLine: About a minute of problems, quick fixes, suggestions, parameter hints, the Docs panel and Try it.

sections.md:
- Open a handler. The extension recognises a .js file in a `handlers` folder, and any other .js file that looks like a handler. From then on it's checked while you type, with problems underlined in the code and listed in the Problems panel.
- Press `Ctrl+.` on a problem to see its fixes. Hover a name to read its docs, and follow the link in the hover if you want the Nucleus Docs panel open beside your code.
- If you don't have a handler yet, **Nucleus: New Handler…** starts one from a template, with your game's name and .exe filled in.
- `F5` steps through the handler in Run and Debug, with breakpoints and the variables for each player.
- **Nucleus: Test in Nucleus Co-op** installs the handler and starts Nucleus with the game selected. Nucleus only reads handlers when it starts, so if it's already open you're asked before it gets closed.
- Everything else is in the command palette. Press `Ctrl+Shift+P` and type "Nucleus".

Some options have no official docs, so an AI wrote theirs from the Nucleus source. In hovers those parts start with ✨, and the Docs panel shows them in a tinted frame.

tools.refNote: These lists are generated from the extension's `package.json`.

tools.title: Notepad++
tools.desc: What the Notepad++ plugin does, and what's in its menu.
tools.what: A plugin for Notepad++, which came first when we asked handler authors what they write in. It underlines problems while you type, fixes them with Alt+Enter, suggests names and shows docs when you hover. Try it, the Hub, packaging and testing in Nucleus Co-op are in its menu.
when: You already write handlers in Notepad++ and see no reason to switch.
You like a light editor. Setup is a double-click on `ncdev.exe`.
You want Install and Test in Nucleus Co-op in a menu.
tools.not: There's no debugger in the plugin. To step through a handler, use VS Code or the workbench.
tools.videoLine: Under a minute. The same checks, fixes, suggestions and docs, plus the plugin's menu.

sections.md:
1. Download `ncdev.exe` from [Get the tools](@site:tools/#get-notepadpp) and close Notepad++.
2. Double-click `ncdev.exe` and choose **Set up Notepad++**. Allow it when Windows asks for permission. (In a terminal, the same thing is `ncdev setup notepad++`.)
3. Open a handler in Notepad++. The plugin's menu is **Plugins › Nucleus Co-op handlers**.

Setup adds the plugin to Notepad++'s `plugins\NcDev` folder and keeps a copy of ncdev in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ncdev`. It doesn't change anything else.

- The plugin runs `ncdev` in the background and asks it about the handler you have open. That's why Notepad++ shows the same problems and docs as the other tools.
- Problems get underlined while you type. Hover one to read what's wrong, or press `Alt+Enter` to fix it.
- **New handler…** in the menu starts one from a template if you don't have one yet.
- **Test in Nucleus Co-op** installs the handler and starts Nucleus with the game selected. Nucleus only reads handlers when it starts, so if it's already open you're asked before it gets closed.
- The rest is in the menu too, under **Plugins › Nucleus Co-op handlers**.

Some options have no official docs, so an AI wrote theirs from the Nucleus source. Notepad++ marks those with [AI].

tools.refNote: This list is read from the plugin's own menu.

tools.title: Other editors
tools.what: `ncdev lsp` is a language server for handlers. That's a small program your editor runs in the background and asks for problems, suggestions and docs. Any editor with language-server support gets the same checks, fixes, hover docs, outline and formatting as VS Code. If it also has a debug client, `ncdev dap` adds the debugger.
when: You use Neovim, Helix, Emacs, Kate, Sublime Text, a JetBrains IDE or Zed and want to keep using it.
You don't mind adding a few lines to your editor's config.
Your editor isn't on the list but has a language-server client. The same server works there.
tools.not: Fair warning: only some of these setups have been tested so far. [Compare the editors](@docs:tools/editors) says which. Notepad++ and VS Code have their own pages.

pair.caption: Your editor starts `ncdev lsp` and talks to it while you type. The server works out what's wrong with the handler, and your editor displays it.

sections.md:
The snippets below start `ncdev` by name, so it has to be on your PATH ([getting ncdev](@docs:tools/ncdev#getting-it)).

Most of them also turn on `compareWithHub`. That makes the server ask hub.splitscreen.me whether a handler from the Hub still has the Hub's `Game.GUID`. Leave that line out if you'd rather it didn't.

The setups come from [PORTING.md]({repo}/blob/main/PORTING.md), which also explains how to port the tools to an editor we don't cover yet. You can see [who has tried each one](@docs:tools/editors#language-server-editors).

tools.title: ncdev (command line)
tools.desc: What ncdev is for, with every command and option.
tools.what: `ncdev` is the command-line version of the tools, in one program. It checks and formats handlers, looks things up in the API, runs Try it and the debugger in a terminal, packages and installs handlers, starts Nucleus Co-op for a test, and searches the Hub. Notepad++ and the other editors run it in the background (`ncdev lsp`), and AI agents connect to it (`ncdev mcp`).
when: You want to check a whole folder of handlers in one go, for example from a script.
You want a quick answer without opening an editor, like `ncdev api KillMutex`.
You're setting up Notepad++ or another editor. They need it.
You're connecting an AI agent to the tools.
tools.not: The workbench and the VS Code extension don't need `ncdev`. If you only use those, you can skip this page.

get.label: Get the tools: the command line

sections.md:
- On Windows, download `ncdev.exe`. On Linux (x64), download `ncdev-linux-x64`, make it runnable and name it `ncdev`. Neither needs anything else installed. Both are on [Get the tools](@site:tools/#command-line).
- On a Mac or ARM Linux, use `nucleus.js` from the same page with Node.js 18 or newer, and write `node nucleus.js` wherever these pages say `ncdev`.
- The editor setups start it by name, so put it in a folder that's on your PATH.
- `ncdev update` fetches the newest version of the standalone program.

- `ncdev lint handlers/` checks every handler in a folder, and exits with an error code if one of them has errors. That's what a script needs to stop on a broken handler.
- `ncdev simulate handler.js --players 3` is Try it in a terminal. It prints each player's window, launch arguments and file changes.
- Add `--help` after a command to see only that command's part of the help.

tools.title: MCP server (AI agents)
tools.desc: What the MCP server gives AI agents, tool by tool.
tools.what: `ncdev mcp` lets an AI agent use the handler tools itself. It speaks MCP (the Model Context Protocol), which is how agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Copilot connect to outside tools. The agent can look up what the API really has, check the handler it wrote, run Try it on it and ask what a line does, so it doesn't have to guess at option names.
when: You write handlers with Claude Code, Codex, Copilot or some other agent that speaks MCP.
You'd like the handler to pass Check before the agent shows it to you.
tools.not: Chatbots without tools, like ChatGPT or Claude in a browser tab, can't use it. For those there's a prompt to paste on [Set up your AI](@site:ai/). And if you write handlers yourself, you don't need this page at all.

b: looks things up, checks, runs Try it
pair.caption: The agent starts `ncdev mcp` and calls the tools below as it works. The prompt on [Set up your AI](@site:ai/) tells it to look a name up before using it and to run Check before it shows you the handler.

sections.md:
It's a normal MCP server over stdio. The command is `ncdev mcp` ([getting ncdev](@docs:tools/ncdev#getting-it)).

- Claude Code: `claude mcp add nucleus -- ncdev mcp`, or install the plugin from [Set up your AI](@site:ai/), which sets it up for you.
- Claude Desktop, Cursor and others with an `mcpServers` list: add the entry below.
- VS Code: nothing to do. The extension registers the server for Copilot and other agents.

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "nucleus": { "command": "ncdev", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

Without the standalone ncdev, use `"command": "node", "args": ["/path/to/nucleus.js", "mcp"]`.

tools.refIntro: The descriptions below are the ones the agent reads, so they're written for it.
tools.refNote: This list comes straight from what `ncdev mcp` serves.
